academic_passage|router.title: Urban Heat Islands
academic_passage|router.passage: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. The main cause is the replacement of vegetation and soil with materials such as asphalt, concrete and brick. These surfaces absorb large amounts of solar energy during the day and release it slowly at night, which keeps urban temperatures high even after sunset. In addition, cars, air conditioners and factories produce heat directly, and tall buildings can block winds that would otherwise carry warm air away. The effect is not merely uncomfortable. Higher temperatures increase the demand for electricity, worsen air quality and can be dangerous for elderly people during heat waves. For this reason, many cities are experimenting with solutions. Some paint roofs white or light gray so that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Others plant trees along streets, since leaves provide shade and release water vapor that cools the air. Green roofs, which are covered with plants, offer similar benefits and can also reduce flooding by holding rainwater. Researchers note, however, that the best combination of strategies depends on each city's climate, layout and budget.

academic_passage|router.title: How Honeybees Share Directions
academic_passage|router.passage: When a honeybee discovers a rich source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a series of movements that scientists call the waggle dance. The dance takes place on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, usually in complete darkness, so other bees follow it by touch and vibration rather than by sight. During the dance, the bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. The angle of the straight run in relation to vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the position of the sun. For example, a run pointing straight up tells the other bees to fly directly toward the sun. The length of the waggle run communicates distance: the longer the run lasts, the farther away the food is. Remarkably, bees adjust their dance as the sun moves across the sky during the day. Experiments in which researchers moved feeding stations to new locations confirmed that bees recruited by the dance search mainly in the indicated area. This system allows a colony to direct its foragers efficiently toward the best flowers, an important advantage when food is scattered and changes with the seasons.

academic_passage|easy.title: The Early History of the Bicycle
academic_passage|easy.passage: The bicycle is so common today that it is easy to forget it was once a new invention. One of the first machines was built in Germany in 1817. It was made of wood and had two wheels, but it had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed the ground with their feet. People called it a running machine. About fifty years later, inventors in France added pedals to the front wheel. This made riding faster, but the ride was very uncomfortable, and many people called these bicycles boneshakers. Later, builders made the front wheel very large so that each turn of the pedals carried the rider farther. These high-wheel bicycles were fast, but they were also dangerous, because riders sat high above the ground and could fall easily. In the 1880s, a new design solved many of these problems. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. Soon, rubber tires filled with air made the ride much smoother. This safety bicycle quickly became popular, and its basic shape is still used today. The bicycle gave many people, including women, a new kind of freedom to travel.

academic_passage|easy.title: Why Sleep Matters
academic_passage|easy.passage: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep each night, but many people sleep less because of work, study or screens. Scientists have learned that sleep is not just a time when the body rests. While we sleep, the brain is very busy. One of its jobs is to organize memories. Information we learned during the day is moved and stored so that we can use it later. This is why students who sleep well after studying often remember more than students who stay up all night. Sleep also helps the body repair itself. During deep sleep, the body produces substances that help muscles grow and heal. In addition, a good night of sleep helps protect us from illness, because it makes the body's defense system stronger. When people do not sleep enough, they often feel tired and find it hard to pay attention. They may also feel more stressed or become angry more easily. Experts give simple advice for better sleep. They suggest going to bed at the same time every night, keeping the bedroom dark and quiet, and avoiding phones and computers before bed. Even small changes can make a big difference.
